meta.titre: Matrix Transformations: Images, Fixed Points and Invariant Lines
meta.sous_theme: Image of a point under a matrix, invariant points, invariant lines

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Additional Mathematics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: When a graphic designer in Douala reflects a logo in a mirror line, every point on the mirror line stays exactly where it was, while all the other points move. In Additional Mathematics a 2 by 2 matrix plays the role of such a movement, and the GCE asks which points or which lines the transformation leaves unchanged. The work is a short piece of algebra: set the image equal to the object and solve. Because the equations are simple, the marks are lost only through careless setting out or a missed second answer.

items: A $2\times 2$ matrix times a column vector: $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}ax+by\\cx+dy\end{pmatrix}$.
The origin $(0,0)$ is mapped to itself by every matrix transformation.
A line through the origin has an equation of the form $y=mx$.
Simultaneous linear equations are solved by elimination or substitution, and a quadratic equation by factorising.

sections.titre: Images, invariant points and invariant lines
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Image of a point

The transformation $T$ with matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ sends the point $(x,y)$ to the point $(x',y')=(ax+by,\ cx+dy)$. The point $(x',y')$ is the **image** and $(x,y)$ is the **object**. To find the object from an image, solve the two equations $ax+by=x'$ and $cx+dy=y'$.

### Invariant points

A point is **invariant** when it is its own image. Then $ax+by=x$ and $cx+dy=y$, that is,

$$
(a-1)x+by=0,\qquad cx+(d-1)y=0 \tag{1}
$$

The origin always satisfies these equations. If the two equations are really the same equation (this happens when $(a-1)(d-1)-bc=0$ and the matrix is not the identity), every point on one line through the origin is invariant: this line is a **line of invariant points**. Otherwise the origin is the only invariant point.

### Invariant lines

A line is **invariant** when each point of the line is mapped to a point of the same line. The points may move along it, so an invariant line is not the same as a line of invariant points. For a line through the origin, take a general point $(x,mx)$ on $y=mx$. Its image is $\big((a+bm)x,\ (c+dm)x\big)$. This lies on $y=mx$ when $c+dm=m(a+bm)$, that is,

$$
bm^{2}+(a-d)m-c=0 \tag{2}
$$

Solve the quadratic for $m$: each root gives an invariant line $y=mx$. When $b=0$, the line $x=0$ is also invariant, since $(0,y)$ is mapped to $(0,dy)$.

variantes.nom: Finding the image or the object
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a point and the matrix are given, or an image and the matrix.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For an image, multiply the matrix by the column of the point. For the object whose image is $(x',y')$, write $ax+by=x'$ and $cx+dy=y'$ and solve them as simultaneous equations.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When equations (1) reduce to a single equation.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If the two equations in (1) are multiples of each other, the invariant points form a line. For $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ the equations are $x+y=0$ and $2x+2y=0$, the same equation, so every point of the line $y=-x$ is invariant.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks for the equation of an invariant line.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use (2), solve the quadratic for $m$ and write each line as $y=mx$. Check one root by taking a point such as $(1,m)$ and verifying that its image has $y'=mx'$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A transformation $T$ is represented by the matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the image of the point $(2,-1)$. (b) Show that the origin is the only invariant point of $T$. (c) Find the equations of the invariant lines of $T$ of the form $y=mx$.

etapes.justification: Multiply the matrix by the column vector.

etapes.action: Set the image equal to the object.

etapes.justification: The first equation gives $2y=0$. Put $y=0$ in the second.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $y=0$, then $3x=0$ so $x=0$. The only invariant point is $(0,0)$.

etapes.justification: The point $(x,mx)$ goes to $\big((1+2m)x,\ 3x\big)$. It is on $y=mx$ if $3=m(1+2m)$.
Take a point on each line and find its image.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The image is $(0,6)$. (b) Solving $x+2y=x$ and $3x=y$ gives only $(0,0)$. (c) The invariant lines of the form $y=mx$ are $y=x$ and $y=-\dfrac{3}{2}x$.

items.erreur_markdown: Looking for invariant points by solving $M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: That equation only gives the origin when the matrix is invertible. An invariant point has image **equal to the object**, not equal to the origin.

items.erreur_markdown: Multiplying in the wrong order, using $(x,y)\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ instead of the matrix times the column.
items.pourquoi_faux: For this course the matrix goes in front of the column vector, so the first row gives $ax+by$. Reversing the order gives $ax+cy$ for the first coordinate.

items.erreur_markdown: Finding $m=1$ and forgetting the second root of the quadratic.
items.pourquoi_faux: A quadratic has up to two roots, and the transformation can have two invariant lines. Writing one loses a mark.
items.correction_markdown: Factorise or use the formula to get both roots, then write both lines.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that a line of invariant points and an invariant line are the same thing.
items.pourquoi_faux: On a line of invariant points every point stays where it is. On an invariant line the points may move, as long as they stay on the line.
items.correction_markdown: Check the point itself first (image equals object), then only the line (image on the line).

items.erreur_markdown: Writing the equation of an invariant line as $y=mx+c$ with any $c$ when the line passes through the origin.
items.pourquoi_faux: A line through the origin has $c=0$. Adding a constant describes a different line and the derivation of (2) no longer applies.
items.correction_markdown: Write $y=mx$ for the lines through the origin.

items.enonce_markdown: A transformation is represented by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$. Find (a) the image of the point $(-1,4)$, and (b) the point whose image is $(8,0)$.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-3+4\\-1+12\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\11\end{pmatrix}$. (b) Let the object be $(x,y)$. Then $3x+y=8$ and $x+3y=0$. The second gives $x=-3y$, so $-9y+y=8$, $y=-1$ and $x=3$. Check: $3(3)+(-1)=8$ and $3+3(-1)=0$. **(a) $(1,11)$; (b) $(3,-1)$.**

items.enonce_markdown: Find all the invariant points of the transformation with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
items.solution_markdown: Set $2x+y=x$ and $2x+3y=y$. The first gives $x+y=0$. The second gives $2x+2y=0$, which is the same equation. So every point with $y=-x$ is invariant, for example $(1,-1)$ is mapped to $(2-1,\ 2-3)=(1,-1)$. **The invariant points form the line $y=-x$.**

items.enonce_markdown: A transformation is represented by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. (a) Find the equations of the invariant lines of the form $y=mx$. (b) Find the image of the point $(3,3)$ and say what this shows.
items.solution_markdown: (a) The point $(x,mx)$ goes to $\big((4+m)x,\ (2+3m)x\big)$. It is on $y=mx$ when $2+3m=m(4+m)$, so $m^{2}+m-2=0$, $(m+2)(m-1)=0$ and $m=1$ or $m=-2$. (b) $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}15\\15\end{pmatrix}$. The point $(3,3)$ moves to $(15,15)$, which is still on $y=x$: the line is invariant but its points are not fixed. **(a) $y=x$ and $y=-2x$; (b) $(15,15)$.**

items_markdown: The image of $(x,y)$ under $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ is $(ax+by,\ cx+dy)$; the matrix is written in front of the column.
An invariant point has image **equal to itself**: solve $(a-1)x+by=0$ and $cx+(d-1)y=0$. The origin is always invariant.
If the two equations are the same equation, a whole line of points is invariant.
An invariant line may have points that move along it. For $y=mx$ solve $bm^{2}+(a-d)m-c=0$ and give every root.
Check an invariant line by taking one point on it and testing that its image stays on the line.
